In 'Walk to Nibbana', what is the primary Dhamma theme and practical guidance offered?

In 'Walk to Nibbana', the teaching opens with this observation: *"Pothgulgala Dhamagrantha 
Dharmasravana Mādhya Bhāraya 
 
 This is to inform our readers that all 
Dhamma books so far written and yet to 
be written by Venerable Bhikkhu 
Kaṭukurunde Ñā ṇananda will hereafter 
be published by the P.D.D.M.B (Kandy) 
and that the D.G.M.B."* The central invitation is to turn one's investigation inward — to verify the Dhamma not as an external philosophy, but as directly observable reality in one's own body, speech, and mind. As the text emphasizes, the Dhamma is *akāliko* (timeless) and *opanayiko* (leading inward), realizable (*paccattaṁ*) by each practitioner through patient, honest awareness.

How does 'Walk to Nibbana' explain the role of dukkha (suffering (dukkha)) in meditation?

In 'Walk to Nibbana', dukkha is discussed in this context: *"Attending to the breath in the case of ānāpānasati and fixing the 
mind on the visual sign that occurs in the light of the Three 
Signata (impermanence, suffering and not -self) in the case of 
such cemetery meditations like the skeleton, the bloated corpse, 
and the livid corpse, could usher in insight ."* Here, dukkha (suffering (dukkha)) is treated not as a theoretical doctrine, but as a living faculty to be actively cultivated and observed. When we bring genuine mindfulness to our direct experience, the quality of dukkha helps dismantle habitual delusion and stabilizes the mind in clear, unentangled awareness.

In 'Walk to Nibbana', how are we advised to handle suffering (dukkha) and emotional stress?

The text teaches: *"Attending to the breath in the case of ānāpānasati and fixing the 
mind on the visual sign that occurs in the light of the Three 
Signata (impermanence, suffering and not -self) in the case of 
such cemetery meditations like the skeleton, the bloated corpse, 
and the livid corpse, could usher in insight ."* Rather than running away from discomfort or trying to suppress it, the Thai Forest approach is to turn around and investigate suffering directly (*dukkha-sacca*). Notice that suffering is not a permanent fixture of the heart; it is a conditioned experience arising from attachment and craving (*taṇhā*). When observed with still, patient awareness, the knot of tension naturally unwinds.

How does 'Walk to Nibbana' characterize the nature of consciousness and the knowing mind?

The text observes: *"Then one can call to mind a term like ‘ Arahaṁ’ or ‘ Buddho’ in 
the case of ‘Recollection of the Buddha’ ( Buddhānussati) or a 
phrase like ‘May you be happy!’ in the case of meditation on 
‘Universal Love’ or Mettā, an d continue pacing up and down 
with unbroken mindfulness attending to it."* Consciousness (*viññāṇa*) is not an independent 'soul' or enduring self; it arises in dependence on contact (*phassa*) and sense objects. The practice is to distinguish between the passing objects of awareness (thoughts, feelings, sensations) and the pure, unattached quality of 'the one who knows' (*poo roo*), resting in unconditioned peace.

What specific meditation instructions on breath awareness are given in 'Walk to Nibbana'?

The text instructs: *"6       
 Although ‘ānāpānasati’ (‘Mindfulness of Breathing’) is a 
meditation specially meant for the seated posture, one who has 
practised it for a long time can arouse it  even in the caṅkamana."* Working with the breath (*ānāpānasati*) serves as both an anchor for tranquility (*samatha*) and a foundation for discernment (*vipassanā*). Allow the breath to flow naturally without force — observe where the sensation is felt most clearly, and maintain continuous, relaxed presence with each in-and-out breath.

In 'Walk to Nibbana', what insight is conveyed by the reflection on: 'journey Nibbāna also ‘Four-wheeled...'?

The text reflects: *"The journey to 
Nibbāna is also a ‘Four-wheeled Drive.’  
 The Buddha has clearly ex plained to us how these four -
wheels are made to roll towards Nibbāna in the sub -section on 
postures in the section on body-contemplation in the Satipaṭṭhāna 
Sutta."* This passage points directly to the heart of experiential practice: letting go of superficial concepts and tuning awareness to the immediate truth of the moment. By investigating experience with honesty and forbearance (*khanti*), we discover an unshakable inner refuge that remains undisturbed by the worldly winds.
